title: Inside The Lab Growing Mutant Bacteria To Terraform Earth | NOEMA
gist: Ricard Solé's Complex Systems Lab in Barcelona is 'hardening' and CRISPR-editing dryland cyanobacteria to make them secrete hyaluronic acid that traps soil moisture, betting that engineering the ecosystem's existing engineers is a cheaper, more conservative planetary intervention than geoengineering. The article reports the first realistic mesocosm test of whether synthetic microbes wreck real ecosystems, and marks a regulatory turning point: an IUCN blanket ban on wild GMO release failed by a single vote in Abu Dhabi.

themes.theme: Hardening as a microbial selection pipeline

insights.claim: A Barcelona lab has cut an initial 70 species of photosynthetic bacteria collected from arid soil near Alicante down to just 16 survivors by subjecting samples to three years of artificial drought, heat and ultraviolet cycles, a process called 'hardening'.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Directed-selection pipelines can produce climate-tolerant biological inputs without gene editing, sidestepping GMO regulation entirely — a faster commercial path than CRISPR products.
insights.quote: So far, Conde Pueyo has whittled down an initial 70 species of photosynthetic bacteria from the sample to just 16
insights.locator: So far, Conde Pueyo has whittled

insights.claim: Stress-hardening does not merely select tougher microbes but appears to change them: hardened Microcoleus vaginatus began building elaborate hand-shaped filament architectures never previously observed in the strain, which researchers attribute to genome changes induced by the ordeal.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: If stress regimes generate novel functional traits, cheap environmental conditioning becomes a discovery engine competing with expensive synthetic-biology design cycles.
insights.quote: I think it’s because we’ve changed the genome
insights.locator: The UV blasts and drought-like conditions

insights.claim: Growing billions of pre-adapted, heat- and aridity-tolerant soil bacteria creates a 'dryland probiotic' that is shovel-ready today, importing organisms from the future climate into the present rather than waiting for evolution.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: A non-GMO 'probiotic' product is the near-term commercializable asset in this space; gene-edited versions are the option value behind it.
insights.quote: take species from the future and you bring it back to now
insights.locator: Rather than waiting for a species to evolve resistance

insights.claim: Drylands make up more than 40% of terrestrial Earth — roughly six times the area of Canada — and support more than 2 billion people, up to 44% of world agriculture and about one-third of global biodiversity hotspots.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: The exposed asset base for desertification risk is far larger than commonly modeled: nearly half of global agricultural output sits on land subject to abrupt, irreversible state change.
insights.locator: Drylands — arid environments ranging from

insights.claim: Drylands do not degrade gradually — they absorb increasing aridity with little visible impact and then collapse suddenly, passing three discrete catastrophic thresholds ending in an 'ecosystem breakdown phase' where rainfall replenishes only about one-fifth of what evaporation removes.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Nonlinearity means agricultural and insurance risk in arid regions is systematically underpriced until it repriceable overnight; leading indicators must come from soil microbiology, not yield trends.
insights.quote: Drylands initially withstood the increased aridity with little impact, then collapsed suddenly.
insights.locator: The results were alarming

insights.claim: Half of the planet's drylands — 20% of Earth's land — are predicted to pass at least one desertification threshold by 2100, and these transitions do not reverse when cooling and rains return.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Hysteresis means mitigation-only climate strategies cannot restore lost land productivity; restoration technology becomes a structurally required category rather than optional.
insights.locator: As climate changes and droughts deepen

insights.claim: Drylands store 46% of the world's terrestrial carbon, so as these soils dry out they flip from carbon sinks to net emitters.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: A feedback that converts nearly half of land carbon storage into emissions undermines the sink assumptions embedded in most net-zero pathways and carbon-credit accounting.
insights.quote: Collectively, drylands store 46% of the world’s terrestrial carbon, and as these carbon sinks dry, they become net emitters.
insights.locator: This can mean devastation for local communities

insights.claim: Spanish government-backed research finds that 40% of Spain is following Alicante's path toward desertification, following heatwaves, prolonged droughts and 2024 flash floods that killed hundreds.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Southern European land, water and agricultural assets face a documented sovereign-scale degradation trend, with adaptation spending likely to follow.
insights.locator: Southeastern Spain has already been hard hit

insights.claim: Roughly 12 million hectares of drylands are degraded every year as part of a global reshuffle in which humid areas become drylands and drylands become deserts.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: An annual land-loss run rate of this size sets a floor on demand for restoration inputs, irrigation technology and climate migration policy.
insights.locator: Already, 12 million hectares of drylands

insights.claim: Earth passed its first planetary tipping point during the past year at 1.4 degrees Celsius of warming, when warm-water coral reefs began collapsing worldwide, threatening the quarter of fish species living on reefs and the billion people who depend on them.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: The first confirmed planetary threshold crossing shifts the policy conversation from prevention to intervention, opening budget for previously taboo technologies.
insights.locator: In the last year, as we reached 1.4 degrees

insights.claim: Ricard Solé's terraforming approach rejects grandiose geoengineering — space mirrors, aerosol-spraying aircraft fleets — on the grounds that nature has already evolved self-sustaining, self-replicating machines that only need to be extracted and improved.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Biological intervention has orders-of-magnitude lower capex than solar radiation management, making it the likelier destination for climate-intervention capital if regulation loosens.
insights.quote: So we engineer the ecosystem engineers — that’s kind of the trick
insights.locator: Solé's approach treats ecological systems

insights.claim: A single CRISPR tweak can make soil cyanobacteria convert ambient moisture into a trail of hyaluronic acid — the same goo used by the cosmetics industry — letting the microbes hydrate soil as they migrate through it.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: The active mechanism is a known, already-manufactured biopolymer, which lowers technical and regulatory novelty risk versus de novo synthetic pathways.
insights.locator: His lab has already shown it is possible

insights.claim: Solé models dryland restoration as a 'synthetic mutualistic loop' that is multiplicative rather than additive: an engineered strain improves soil quality, better soil raises plant cover, and plant cover feeds back into soil quality.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Positive-feedback restoration implies small, cheap interventions can carry disproportionate returns — the economic case rests on leverage, not on scale of dosing.
insights.quote: the hope is our synthetic strain will improve soil quality; soil quality improves plant cover; and plant cover improves soil quality
insights.locator: A small change in moisture levels

insights.claim: Cyanobacteria can account for up to 95% of the biomass in dryland soil, binding dust with filaments and sticky exopolysaccharides as the pioneer species that eventually permits lichens, mosses, vascular plants and trees.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Concentration of biomass in one organism class means a single microbial intervention has an unusually high share of the system's total leverage.
insights.locator: The pioneers are typically cyanobacteria

insights.claim: Postdoc Victor Maull has built genetic circuits to make bacteria produce hyaluronic acid that are ready for testing in the model organism Bacillus subtilis, meaning the goo-producing trait is at lab-validation stage rather than concept stage.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Concrete technology-readiness marker: the bottleneck is ecosystem validation and regulation, not the underlying genetic engineering.
insights.locator: Maull has developed “genetic circuits”

insights.claim: The Synterra project has built a climate-controlled replica of the Alicante dryland roughly the size of a fridge-freezer, reproducing that region's actual humidity, rain, temperature and UV on a one-month-and-twelve-hour lag using real weather data.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: A validated digital-physical twin of an ecosystem is the missing test rig that could unlock regulatory approval for wild release — watch it as the gating milestone.
insights.locator: Today, the mesocosm traps the soil microbes

insights.claim: EMBL Barcelona's James Sharpe framed the dryland mesocosm explicitly as an ecological analogue of human organoids — a halfway house between single-cell experiments and full test subjects — importing biomedical experimental standards into ecology.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Borrowing the organoid paradigm gives ecological intervention a credible preclinical stage, the same structural step that made drug development investable.
insights.quote: ecosystem in vitro
insights.locator: The developmental biologist James Sharpe

insights.claim: All of the Complex Systems Lab's computer models so far show synthetic bacteria remain safely controlled without any engineered kill switch, because microbes can be programmed to activate only under narrow conditions such as a defined dryness level and die once the soil is rehydrated.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: If containment can be achieved by environmental conditionality rather than engineered kill switches, a major cost and failure mode of biocontainment disappears.
insights.locator: All the Complex Systems Lab's computer models

insights.claim: Because the 1980s GMO backlash chilled research, there is almost no empirical data on how synthetic microbes interact with wider ecosystems — Solé calls the field 'terra incognita'.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Decades of regulatory chill created an evidence vacuum that now cuts both ways: no proof of harm, but also no data to license deployment at scale.
insights.quote: It’s terra incognita
insights.locator: So far they're reliant on computer models

themes.theme: Biodiversity as firewall — the risk argument

insights.claim: Solé argues that 99% of introduced organisms never become runaway problems and that biodiversity itself acts as a firewall containing new arrivals, making invasive species like Australia's cane toads rare exceptions rather than the base case.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Reframing invasion risk as a low-base-rate tail rather than the default expectation is the argument that could shift regulatory posture on wild release.
insights.quote: Biodiversity is a strong firewall that can contain and control things
insights.locator: But Solé has argued that diverse ecosystems

insights.claim: Horizontal gene transfer, usually cited as the danger that could spread engineered traits to unrelated species, can instead be exploited as a safety asset by carrying the goo-producing trait on an ejectable plasmid rather than editing the bacterium's core chromosomal DNA.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Plasmid-based delivery is a reversibility mechanism that could become the design standard regulators demand for environmental release.
insights.locator: In work with microbiologist Victor de Lorenzo

insights.claim: Solé poses a double-standard challenge: shipping tons of exotic soil and haystacks with entirely foreign microbiomes, as in China's Tengger Desert labor-heavy approach, is accepted, while adding a single gene to a cyanobacterium already native to the community is treated as unacceptable.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: The comparative-risk framing is the rhetorical wedge most likely to break the wild-release veto — watch for it in regulatory filings and NGO debate.
insights.quote: But “a single gene, put in a cyanobacteria that was [already] in the community, is a problem?
insights.locator: Solé asks what the public would prefer

insights.claim: Kent Redford argues that self-propagating solutions are precisely what effective conservation now requires, and that this necessity is exactly what frightens the public most.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: The scaling logic of biological intervention is inseparable from its containment risk — no solution scales cheaply without also being harder to recall.
insights.quote: And that need to have self-propagating solutions is even scarier to people.
insights.locator: Critics have warned that, if rats escaped

themes.theme: The Abu Dhabi vote — regulatory inflection

insights.claim: At the IUCN World Conservation Congress in Abu Dhabi last October, a proposed blanket ban on releasing genetically modified organisms into the wild failed by a single vote after more than 250 scientists signed a letter defending synthetic biology.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: A one-vote margin is the single most tradeable fact here: the wild-release regime for engineered organisms is at a knife-edge and could flip either way at the next congress.
insights.quote: The final tally was split nearly perfectly, and the ban failed by a single vote, paving the way toward the release of synthetic organisms into the wild.
insights.locator: A key vote in Abu Dhabi

insights.claim: Synthetic biology has shifted from fringe to mainstream within conservation over a decade, with practitioners in reefs, forests and the Arctic tundra now adopting it — Solé notes 'We are not, anymore, these crazy guys saying crazy things.'
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Institutional legitimacy is the precondition for funding; the sector's Overton window moved before the technology did.
insights.quote: We are not, anymore, these crazy guys saying crazy things
insights.locator: In the decade that Solé has traveled to speak

insights.claim: Roughly 90% of coral reefs face extinction by 2050, pushing environmentalists toward gene editing, small-scale geoengineering and other interventions they previously rejected.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Crisis-driven acceptance is the demand mechanism for intervention technologies: the worse the ecological data, the faster the regulatory door opens.
insights.locator: Reefs show us the way

insights.claim: Africa's Great Green Wall, launched in 2007 as a 10-mile-wide, 5,000-mile belt of trees across the Sahel, has made little progress in nearly two decades, with an estimated 80% of millions of planted trees dying in some areas.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: The flagship megaproject's failure rate is the strongest evidence that tree-count-based restoration metrics and the credits built on them are unreliable.
insights.locator: This ecological megaproject began in 2007

insights.claim: China's Tengger Desert green wall also suffered mass tree mortality initially but recovered over 30 years by inventing a 'checkerboard' technique that half-buries straw in a grid to anchor sand and adds manure in the centers, demonstrating that soil comes before trees.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Successful restoration is a soil-engineering problem with a decades-long payback, not a planting problem — reprice restoration timelines accordingly.
insights.locator: China's own green wall project in the Tengger Desert

insights.claim: Only about half a dozen labs worldwide — in Spain, China, Australia and the U.S. — are researching biocrust-driven restoration, with the world's first 'biocrust farm' near Moab, Utah pioneering the 'soil skin graft' transplant method.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: An extremely thin global research base means IP and expertise concentration risk is high — early positions in biocrust restoration face little competition but also little validation infrastructure.

insights.claim: Restoring and protecting drylands could capture as much as a gigaton of carbon per year, roughly equal to the total nations have committed to capture under the Paris Agreement.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: If credible, dryland restoration is a carbon-removal category of the same order as all Paris commitments combined — a potentially enormous credit supply if measurement can be solved.
insights.locator: It's difficult to say how much carbon could be captured

insights.claim: Researchers in Spain want to repurpose the photovoltaic plants rapidly expanding across global drylands as nurseries for biocrust and plants, because solar arrays create tree-like microclimates of shifting shade.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Solar developers in arid regions may gain a second revenue and permitting lever — land restoration co-benefits bundled with generation assets.
insights.quote: We want to use these photovoltaic farms as nurseries to grow biocrust and plants
insights.locator: Teams in the U.S. and Europe believe

insights.claim: The Almeria pilot is developing lower-cost bacterial feed chemicals, compost made from paper factory waste as a binding additive, and 'biopriming' of seeds in microbes, aiming eventually to spray a ready-made dryland from a hose via hydroseeding.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: The cost curve here depends on waste-stream feedstocks and spray application — the same economics that made agricultural inoculants scalable.
insights.locator: At a pilot in Almeria

themes.theme: Novel ecosystems and the Holocene hallucination

insights.claim: Kent Redford argues that the belief we can keep living in the stable world of the last 10,000 years is a 'holocene hallucination' that flies in the face of all evidence, and that the pre-Anthropocene world cannot be recovered.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: If baseline restoration is impossible, conservation budgets shift from preservation toward design and adaptation — a different vendor set entirely.
insights.quote: Most of us continue to believe that we can continue to live in the relatively stable world we’ve lived in for 10,000 years or more, but this is a kind of “holocene hallucination,”
insights.locator: Most of us continue to believe

insights.claim: Forecasts show historically unprecedented 'novel ecosystems' — landscapes pushed into wholly new states by climate change and pollution — could make up more than 50% of terrestrial ecosystems by 2100.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: A majority-novel biosphere invalidates historical-baseline conservation law and offsets methodology, forcing a rewrite of what 'restoration' legally means.
insights.locator: Already, nature reserves are forced to reckon

insights.claim: Ascension Island's man-made cloud forest on Green Mountain — assembled from hundreds of species the British transported there over three decades in the 19th century, on a rock Darwin called a hideous 'cinder' in 1836 — proves that whole ecosystems can be deliberately designed and that biomass and biodiversity can boom as a result.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: A two-century natural experiment gives the design-an-ecosystem thesis empirical cover, which matters more for public acceptance than any lab result.
insights.quote: An old scientific experiment that proves ecosystems can be designed
insights.locator: For Maull, Ascension is

insights.claim: Ascension's transformation worked through the same mechanism the Barcelona lab is engineering at microbial scale — Hooker erected foliage to trap ocean moisture that would otherwise blow past, a macro version of bacteria capturing mist.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Water capture, not carbon or nutrients, is identified as the controlling variable for flipping arid systems into verdant states — the metric to track in any restoration project.
insights.locator: Although far messier than the lab's clinical experiments

insights.claim: Conde Pueyo argues the romanticism of returning ecosystems to an old steady state may need to be abandoned, with Sahel communities forced to invent new ecosystems for a new harsh climate as Ascension's settlers did.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: The intellectual shift from restoration to invention is what unlocks a much larger addressable market for engineered biology in land management.
insights.quote: This romanticism about just going back to the old steady state, maybe it needs to be abandoned.
insights.locator: When the past cannot be maintained

insights.claim: Redford dismisses de-extinction ventures as irrelevant to planetary outcomes while ranking dryland remedies as decisive, drawing a sharp line between charismatic biotech and interventions that change where the world remains habitable.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: A credible authority publicly discounting the highest-profile funded climate-biotech names while elevating an unfunded academic niche is a valuation-relevant signal.
insights.quote: De-extinction, and all of that sort of thing, makes absolutely no difference in the future of the world. It doesn’t matter at all
insights.locator: What sets Solé's microbial solution apart

insights.claim: Redford frames public revulsion toward gene editing and impure landscapes as a 'Mountain Gloom, Mountain Glory' phase, analogous to 17th-century travelers who drew their carriage curtains to avoid seeing the Alps before Romantic writers reversed that aesthetic within a century.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Treating public opposition as a transient aesthetic regime rather than a fixed constraint implies the political ceiling on this technology lifts over decades, not never.
insights.quote: I think we’re in a kind of ‘Mountain Gloom, Mountain Glory’ phase now
insights.locator: It's tough for people to face the fact

insights.claim: Solé points to genetically modified mosquitoes already released in several countries as an effective malaria precaution, arguing a working microbial product would convert doubters faster than argument.
insights.speaker: MATTHEW PONSFORD
insights.so_what: Precedent of deployed GM organisms in public health is the template argument for environmental release approvals.
